claims.claim: Article VIII of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo held that Mexicans remaining in the ceded territory over one year defaulted to US citizenship unless they declared otherwise, and their property was to be respected.
claims.source: treaty text (Avalon Art. VIII); Griswold p.66; NARA
claims.anchor: ### Claim: Article VIII — Mexicans staying >1yr defaulted to US citizenship unless they declared otherwise; property to be respected

claims.claim: The US Senate weakened Article IX before ratification, changing its citizenship-rights timeline from 'as soon as possible' to being decided at the proper time, to be judged of by Congress.
claims.verbatim: at the proper time, to be judged of by Congress
claims.source: Gómez p.130 (verbatim); Griswold p.46; treaty text
claims.anchor: ### Claim: Senate WEAKENED Article IX ("as soon as possible" → "at the proper time, to be judged of by Congress")

claims.claim: The US Senate deleted Article X of the treaty entirely before ratification — the article that would have honored all Spanish and Mexican land grants.
claims.anchor: ### Claim: Senate DELETED Article X entirely (would have honored all Spanish/Mexican land grants)

claims.claim: The 1848 Protocol of Querétaro assured Mexico that striking Article X was not meant to void Mexican-era land grants, a reassurance the United States later disavowed.
claims.source: Ebright pp.29-30; Gómez pp.130-131; Griswold p.54
claims.anchor: ### Claim: Protocol of Querétaro reassured Mexico → US (Sec. Clayton, 1849) disavowed it

claims.claim: In 1849, US Secretary of State John Clayton stated the United States had at no time regarded the Protocol of Querétaro as obligatory, formally disavowing it.
claims.verbatim: at no time regarded the Protocol as obligatory.
claims.anchor: ### Claim: Protocol of Querétaro reassured Mexico → US (Sec. Clayton, 1849) disavowed it

claims.claim: The land-dispossession process ran through a Surveyor General's office created in 1854, then the Court of Private Land Claims (1891-1904), culminating in U.S. v. Sandoval (1897), which held communal lands had belonged to the Mexican sovereign and passed to the United States in 1848.
claims.source: Ebright pp.34-48; Gómez pp.128-134; Sandoval opinion
claims.anchor: ### Claim: Dispossession machine — Surveyor General (1854) → Court of Private Land Claims (1891–1904) → U.S. v. Sandoval (1897) communal-lands doctrine

claims.claim: The Court of Private Land Claims confirmed only about 6% of the acreage claimed under Mexican-era land grants, roughly 35.5 million claimed acres reduced to about 2.05 million confirmed, across 88 confirmed grants out of 291 consolidated cases.
claims.anchor: ### Claim: CPLC confirmed ~6% of acreage claimed (~35.5M→~2.05M); 88 grants/291 cases; CA ~75% vs NM ~6%

claims.claim: California's Mexican-era land grant claims were confirmed at a rate of about 75%, compared to only about 6% in New Mexico.
claims.anchor: ### Claim: CPLC confirmed ~6% of acreage claimed (~35.5M→~2.05M); 88 grants/291 cases; CA ~75% vs NM ~6%

claims.claim: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo contained no clause making the English text prevail over the Spanish; both language versions were signed as equally authentic, following the precedent set in the Percheman case.
claims.anchor: ### Claim: No English-prevails clause; texts equally authentic (Percheman precedent)

claims.claim: Estimates for the population living in the territory Mexico ceded in 1848 range from about 56,000 to about 100,000; no credible source supports the commonly cited figure of 80,000.
claims.anchor: ### Claim: Population of ceded territory — use sourced RANGE, not "80,000"

claims.claim: The claim that the treaty's English version legally prevailed over the Spanish in case of discrepancy is false; the real dispute ran the opposite way, with Mexico invoking the pro-grant Spanish reading via the Protocol of Querétaro, which the US disavowed in 1849.

claims.claim: The San Miguel del Bado land grant originated in 1794 when the Spanish crown granted land to Lorenzo Márquez and 51 other men, and by 1894 it supported over 1,000 families across eight villages.

claims.claim: The Court of Private Land Claims confirmed the San Miguel del Bado grant by a 4-1 vote, but the Supreme Court under Chief Justice Fuller reversed that confirmation in 1897.

claims.claim: Historians disagree on whether the Court of Private Land Claims acted fairly: one scholar called it relatively fair, unbiased, conscientious, while others describe it as being in error, performing national service for US interests, or presiding over a field of pain and death.
